results.title: What is Data Redaction: A Complete Guide for 2026
results.content: Data redaction removes sensitive or confidential information from documents before they are shared with other parties, typically for legal reasons. Redacting documents is often done to protect privacy, trade secrets, and confidential information. Redacting sensitive data is essential to protect confidential information and ensure compliance with laws and regulations. Data redaction is also vital to protect individuals’ personal information. Various types of data need to be redacted to ensure the privacy and security of personal information. When it comes to redacting data, Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is a must. Selective redaction is a data protection technique in which only certain pieces of information, words, or sections are removed from a document. This redaction helps protect the privacy and confidentiality of personal data while still providing enough information to make the document valid. Data redaction keeps data secure and helps protect individuals' privacy by removing personal details from documents. Plus, you'll never have to worry about permanent data loss—because Redactable will ensure your sensitive documents remain safe and secure!

results.title: GitHub - microsoft/synthetic-data-showcase: Generates synthetic data and user interfaces for privacy-preserving data sharing and analysis.
results.content: In this project, we provide an automated set of tools for generating the three elements of a *synthetic data showcase*:. To generate these elements, our tool provides two approaches to create anonymous datasets that are safe to release: (i) differential privacy and (ii) k-anonymity. When applied in the context of private data release, $\varepsilon$ bounds the ratio of probabilities of getting an arbitrary result to an arbitrary computation when using two synthetic datasets – one generated from the sensitive dataset itself and the other from a neighboring dataset missing a single arbitrary record. Our approach to synthesizing data with differential privacy first protects attribute combination counts in the aggregate data using our DP Marginals algorithm and then uses the resulting DP aggregate counts to derive synthetic records that retain differential privacy under the post-processing property. Use of our differential privacy synthesizer is recommended for **repeated data releases** where cumulative privacy loss must be quantified and controlled and where provable guarantees against all possible privacy attacks are desired. When applied in the context of private data release, we interpret k as a privacy resolution determining the minimum group size that will be (a) reported explicitly in the aggregate dataset and (b) represented implicitly by the records of the synthetic dataset. Our approach to synthesizing data with k-anonymity overcomes many of the limitations of standard k-anonymization, in which attributes of sensitive data records are generalized and suppressed until k-anonymity is reached, and only for those attributes determined in advance to be potentially identifying when used in combination (so-called quasi-identifiers). In contrast, our k-anonymity synthesizers generate synthetic records that do not represent actual individuals, yet are composed exclusively from common combinations of attributes in the sensitive dataset. The k-anonymity guarantee therefore holds for all data columns and all combinations of attributes. Use of our k-anonymity synthesizers is recommended only for **one-off data releases** where there is a need for precise counts of attribute combinations (at a given privacy resolution). We provide a set of tools to synthesize, aggregate and evaluate your data, which can be used according to your use case/preference.

results.title: Privacy and Utility of Private Synthetic Data for Medical Data Analyses
results.content: In this paper, we evaluate three different private synthetic data generators (MWEM, DP-CTGAN, and PATE-CTGAN) on their use-case-specific privacy and utility. This work shows that private synthetic data generators have tremendous advantages over traditional techniques, but also require in-depth analysis depending on the use case. synthetic data generation; differential privacy; secondary use; medical data; private data processing; open source framework. We analyze the extent to which privacy is really protected with synthetic data and how high the utility of the data is compared to established technologies such as DP. * Introduction of a use case-specific privacy and utility metric for synthetic medical data;. * Evaluation of three approaches for private synthetic data generation in terms of privacy and utility. While our work addresses a similar research question, we evaluate synthetic data in terms of a specific medical use case where particularly high data accuracy and correlation between different data points is important. The authors compared the approach of generating synthetic data with traditional privacy measures and explained the different legal requirements for private data. While this paper focuses on the utility and usability of synthetic data, we try to consider and evaluate the real-world privacy implications of such techniques in our work. Differential privacy is also presented, as it is used for comparison with synthetic private data generation, which is also outlined in this section. In the following section, we will conduct a plain DP release and use synthetic data technologies to create a private dataset with the same number of entries and individuals. As the name suggests, the latter allows generating synthetic data with three different synthesizers (MWEM, DP-CTGAN, and PATE-CTGAN), which we already described in Section 3.3. A variety of experiments using these metrics were conducted with the three synthetic data generators MWEM, PATE-CTGAN, and DP-CTGAN. In general, synthetic data generators provide a useful way to generate more accurate and private data than a static data release which uses traditional PETs. Finally, it should be considered that the meaning for those technologies is not necessarily the only indicator of privacy and that more use-case-specific metrics are recommended.

results.title: Redaction vs. selective encryption for data protection
results.content: selective encryption for data protection. Redaction has been a favorite technique for information security, but its limitations are many. Selective encryption provides a better way forward for data protection. Traditionally, redaction has been used in scenarios requiring the concealment of specific data within a document, making it ideal for legal, medical, or public documents. For example, in legal documents where personal identifiers must be hidden for privacy or in government reports where sensitive information is redacted for public release. This method provides enhanced data protection over traditional concealment techniques. The effectiveness of Selective Encryption is further amplified when it is coupled with the capability to automatically identify and selectively encrypt sensitive data, thereby eliminating the need for any end-user actions. Without Confidencial's unique Selective Encryption technology, secure and efficient redaction, including partial redaction, would not be feasible while maintaining only a single copy of the document. Encryption secures data from creation to transmission, consumption, and storage. So understanding the nuances between redaction and encryption is vital when protecting sensitive and often unstructured data, as their approaches and effectiveness vary significantly. Method of Sensitive Data Protection. * Redaction is less secure because it can leave traces of the underlying data intact and recoverable for malicious actor use. * Encryption offers a higher level of security by altering the data itself. Even if intercepted, the encrypted data remains secure against cyber-attacks, rendered unreadable and useless. * Encrypting data at the point of creation ensures sensitive information is secured immediately, reducing the risk of unauthorized access from the outset. * Automated encryption solutions, such as those provided by Confidencial, streamline data protection, ensuring consistent and efficient security without manual intervention. While traditional redaction still has its place, the evolution to leveraging advanced and post-quantum-ready encryption marks a pivotal shift in data security. ## Data Protection is due for an upgrade, and Confidencial is ready. As technological threats like quantum computing emerge, robust, automated, and future-oriented protection becomes crucial for effectively navigating and securing sensitive data. *Download our whitepaper, '**Protecting Sensitive Data with Policy-Based Selective Encryption,**' by Karim Eldefrawy, Ph.D., Co-founder and CTO of Confidencial, to learn more about our Selective Encryption.
